title: Cooling Access and the Economics of Climate Adaptation
subtitle: Productivity Preservation, Public Health, Energy Systems, and Economic Resilience in Emerging Economies
dek: Quantifies how passive cooling, high-efficiency solar-coupled air conditioning, and rural cold chains preserve industrial productivity, avert heatwave mortality, and stabilize emerging-economy power grids through 2050.
abstract: As extreme wet-bulb temperatures intensify across the Global South, access to reliable, affordable cooling is transitioning rapidly from a residential amenity into foundational climate-adaptation infrastructure. Anchored to 10 live World Bank World Development Indicators across 24 economies and macro-regions and 24 peer-reviewed studies in labor economics, epidemiology, building physics, and power-systems engineering, this monograph quantifies the macroeconomic returns to sustainable cooling access across emerging economies—linking productivity preservation, public health, clean energy systems, and agricultural-urban resilience.

Live 2024–2025 WDI baselines expose a stark adaptation divide: over 60%–68% of workers in India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, and Sub-Saharan Africa toil in heat-exposed agriculture and industry while operating on just 380 to 1,223 kWh/cap of electricity (versus 7,794 kWh in the OECD and 12,000+ kWh in the United States), even as heat-related labor-capacity losses already exceed USD 1.09 trillion annually worldwide. Modeling an integrated architecture combining passive cool roofs and radiative materials (-30% to -55% thermal loads), doubled-efficiency inverter air conditioning coupled with midday solar PV and phase-change thermal storage, Kigali HFC phase-down, and village agro-cold chains, this study projects a cumulative 2026–2050 Cooling Adaptation Dividend of USD 16 trillion to USD 28 trillion (central: USD 22.0 trillion, constant 2025 USD)—preserving factory and outdoor output, cutting heat mortality by up to 75%, and avoiding grid-peak blackouts and 0.4°C–0.5°C of refrigerant-driven warming by 2100.
findings: Documents the live 2024–2025 emerging-economy heat-adaptation divide (60%–68% heat-exposed workforce on 380–1,223 kWh/cap electricity vs. 7,794 kWh OECD).

Quantifies how passive cooling (-30% to -55% load), high-SEER inverter ACs, midday solar-PV coincidence, and thermal ice storage prevent grid-peak blackouts while cutting cooling energy bills by 40%–60%.

Projects a cumulative 2026–2050 Cooling Adaptation Dividend of USD 16T–28T (central: USD 22.0T) across productivity preservation, public health, grid-peak savings, agro-cold chains, and avoided refrigerant warming.
keywords: passive radiative cooling and urban heat islands
high efficiency air conditioning and Kigali amendment
thermal energy storage and cold chains
method: Empirical synthesis using verified World Bank WDI and international datasets, peer-reviewed literature, H Heuristics Cross-System Spillover (2nd–4th order) mapping, maladaptation guardrails, and quantitative 2050 polycrisis scenarios.
